blocks: Ibuprofen doesn't fix what hurts. It cuts the wire on your body's alarm.
When tissue is injured or inflamed, your cells release a fatty acid and hand it to an enzyme called cyclooxygenase.
That enzyme turns it into prostaglandins, the alarm messengers. They help the area swell, and they make your pain nerves more sensitive.
During an infection, they also reach the part of your brain that sets your temperature, and turn the thermostat up. That's a fever.
Ibuprofen slides into the enzyme's working pocket and blocks it. Fewer prostaglandins means less pain, less swelling, and a lower fever.
The cause is still there. Only the alarm got quieter. And your body clears about half the drug in roughly two hours.
Here's the catch. The same enzyme family also makes prostaglandins that help protect your stomach lining, and ibuprofen blocks those too.

That's why its label warns about stomach bleeding, and about heart attack and stroke risk with higher doses or longer use. Over the counter still means read the label, and ask a pharmacist or doctor if you're unsure.
